title: Affine pushouts along arbitrary scheme thickenings
statement: Let $T,T',S$ be schemes [def-pc-scheme]. Let $i:T\to T'$ be a thickening, meaning a closed immersion inducing a homeomorphism on underlying spaces [def-sbc-first-order-thickening], and let $a:T\to S$ be affine, meaning that the inverse image of every affine open of $S$ is affine. The pushout $P=S\amalg_TT'$ exists in the category of schemes: its maps $j:S\to P$ and $b:T'\to P$ satisfy $ja=bi$, and every compatible pair of scheme morphisms from $S$ and $T'$ to any scheme $Z$ factors uniquely through $P$. The map $j$ is a thickening and the square is cartesian, $T\cong S\times_PT'$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. No finite-order hypothesis is imposed on $i$.

proof.text:
Use the homeomorphism $|i|$ to define the continuous map $a':|T'|\to|S|$ by $a'=|a|\circ|i|^{-1}$. On $|S|$ define a sheaf of rings $\mathcal F$ by
$$\mathcal F(U)=\{(s,t')\in\mathcal O_S(U)\times\mathcal O_{T'}((a')^{-1}U):a^\sharp(s)=i^\sharp(t')\text{ on }a^{-1}U\}.$$
Restrictions and ring operations are coordinatewise. This is a sheaf: a compatible family of pairs glues uniquely in each of the two structure sheaves, and equality of their images holds after gluing because it holds on the covering opens. Thus $P_0=(|S|,\mathcal F)$ is a ringed space. Its construction commutes with restriction to every open $U\subseteq S$, by the displayed formula. We will establish that this explicitly constructed space is a scheme; no scheme is chosen from an existence assertion.

Let $U\subseteq S$ be affine. Set $V=a^{-1}U$ and $V'=(a')^{-1}U$. The affine hypothesis on $a$ makes $V$ affine; the restriction $V\to V'$ is a thickening, since restriction preserves the defining homeomorphism and the surjection of structure sheaves. Hence [lem-weil-pbc-thickening-affine-scheme] makes $V'$ affine without any finite-order assumption. Write $U=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $V'=\operatorname{Spec}A'$ and denote the ring maps by $\beta:B\to A$, $\alpha:A'\twoheadrightarrow A$. Surjectivity of $\alpha$ is the affine characterization in [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Put $C=A'\times_A B$, with projections $p:C\to A'$ and $q:C\to B$. The projection $q$ is surjective: lift $\beta(b)$ along $\alpha$ for each $b\in B$. By [lem-sfb-ring-fibre-product-spectrum], $\operatorname{Spec}C$ is the topological pushout of $V'\leftarrow V\to U$. Since $V\to V'$ is a homeomorphism, $U\to\operatorname{Spec}C$ is a homeomorphism: the identity on $U$ and $a|_V\circ |i|^{-1}$ on $V'$ descend to a continuous inverse, and its other composite is the identity by the quotient description. Thus its inverse identifies $|P_0|_U$ with $|\operatorname{Spec}C|$, compatibly with both projections.

Fix $c=(h',g)\in C$ and put $h=\alpha(h')=\beta(g)$. Under the homeomorphism of step 2, $D_C(c)$ corresponds to $D_B(g)$; its inverse images in $V'$ and $V$ are $D_{A'}(h')$ and $D_A(h)$, since contraction of a prime detects membership of the indicated element. The principal-localization open immersion identifies each such open subscheme with the spectrum of the corresponding localized ring. Its global sections are consequently that localized ring. The definition of $\mathcal F$ and [lem-sfb-ring-fibre-product-spectrum] therefore give
$$\mathcal F(D_B(g))=A'_{h'}\times_{A_h}B_g\cong C_c.$$
These are isomorphisms of rings induced by the localized projections, not only bijections of sets. They commute with further principal localizations by the compatibility clause of the cited node. In particular all these identifications have the same orientation and the same two projection maps.

source.place: Tag 01Z8, lemma-diagram-localize; applied as in Tag 07RT, principal-open structure-sheaf calculation

proof.text: The opens $D_C(c)$ form a basis, and the isomorphisms in step 3 identify the structure sheaf on this basis with $\mathcal F|_U$. To extend them to an arbitrary open, cover it by these basic opens, send a section to its images on them, and glue. On the intersection of two basic opens the comparisons agree: $D_C(c)\cap D_C(d)=D_C(cd)$, and the two restriction maps are the further localizations at $d$ and $c$, respectively. Compatibility with these localizations is precisely the clause used in step 3. This also handles every inclusion $D_C(d)\subseteq D_C(c)$: its intersection is $D_C(cd)=D_C(d)$, so restricting from $D_C(c)$ is the same further localization at $d$, followed by this equality of opens. The same construction with the inverse comparisons gives an inverse sheaf map; the two composites are identities because their restrictions to every basic open are identities. Thus step 2's homeomorphism is an isomorphism of ringed spaces $P_0|_U\cong\operatorname{Spec}C$. Every stalk of $P_0$ is now a local ring, since it is a stalk in one of these affine charts. Affine opens cover $S$, so $P_0$ is locally affine and hence is a scheme $P$ by the definition of a scheme. This proves local affineness for every affine $U$, with no assumption that intersections of affine opens are affine.

The two sheaf projections defining $\mathcal F$ give ringed-space maps $j:S\to P$ and $b:T'\to P$, with underlying maps the identity of $|S|$ and $a'$, respectively. On each affine chart of steps 2--4 they are exactly $\operatorname{Spec}q$ and $\operatorname{Spec}p$, by the localized projection formulas. They are therefore morphisms of schemes: locality of a stalk map is checked in any containing chart, where it is the stalk map of the indicated spectrum morphism. The equality $j\circ a=b\circ i$ follows on sheaf sections from the defining matching condition and on spaces from the definition of $a'$. Moreover $j$ is a homeomorphism and its sheaf map is surjective: over each chart it is induced by the surjection $q:C\to B$, hence is surjective on stalks by the affine closed-immersion characterization. Consequently $j$ is a closed immersion and a thickening. No claim of surjectivity on sections of arbitrary opens is needed.

Let $f:S\to Z$ and $g:T'\to Z$ be scheme morphisms with $f\circ a=g\circ i$, with $Z$ an arbitrary scheme. For each affine $U\subseteq S$, the scheme $P_U=P|_U=\operatorname{Spec}(A'\times_A B)$ and its two maps are the affine pinching diagram. The hypotheses of [lem-sfb-affine-closed-pinching-pushout] hold because $\alpha$ is surjective. Its statement gives a unique morphism $e_U:P_U\to Z$ extending $f|_U$ and $g|_{V'}$. If $W\subseteq U$ is affine, the restriction of $e_U$ to $P_W$ has those same two restrictions, so equals $e_W$ by the uniqueness assertion for the affine pinching diagram at $W$. For two affine opens $U_1,U_2$, cover $U_1\cap U_2$ by affine opens $W$; the affine-basis theorem supplies this cover. The preceding equality and uniqueness in scheme-morphism gluing show that $e_{U_1}$ and $e_{U_2}$ agree on the entire overlap. Scheme-morphism gluing then gives $e:P\to Z$. Its composites with $j$ and $b$ are $f$ and $g$ because this can be checked on the two inverse-image open covers. Any other extension has restriction $e_U$ on every $P_U$ by the affine pushout uniqueness, and hence equals $e$ by gluing uniqueness. This is the required pushout universal property, including nonaffine targets $Z$.

On the affine chart of step 2, put $K=\ker\alpha$ and $J=\ker q=\{(k,0):k\in K\}$. Projection $p$ carries $J$ onto $K$. Consider
$$\mu:A'\otimes_C B\longrightarrow A,\qquad x\otimes b\longmapsto\alpha(x)\beta(b).$$
This is well defined by the balancing relation, since $\alpha p=\beta q$. Define an inverse on $a\in A$ by choosing a lift $x\in A'$ and sending $a$ to $x\otimes1$. If two lifts differ by $k\in K$, then $k\otimes1=1\otimes q(k,0)=0$, so this is independent of the lift. Choosing sums and products of lifts shows that the inverse is additive, multiplicative and unital. Its composite with $\mu$ is the identity on $A$. For the other composite, lift $b\in B$ to $c=(y,b)\in C$, which is possible by surjectivity of $q$; then $x\otimes b=xy\otimes1$, and $xy$ lifts $\alpha(x)\beta(b)$. Thus the other composite fixes every pure tensor and hence every element. This proves $A'\otimes_C B\cong A$ as rings. Its structure maps are exactly $\mu(x\otimes1)=\alpha(x)$ and $\mu(1\otimes b)=\beta(b)$. Conversely, for any lift $y$ of $\beta(b)$, the element $(y,b)\in C$ gives $y\otimes1=1\otimes b$, so the inverse respects the map from $B$ as well as the map from $A'$. This elementary calculation uses only the matching-pair ring and the defining tensor relations, without an exactness theorem or a nilpotence bound.

source.place: Tag 07RT, cartesian-square assertion; explicit tensor calculation on its affine charts

proof.text: Form $R=S\times_P T'$ and the canonical map $\theta:T\to R$ from $a$ and $i$. Over $P_U$, all three schemes $U,V',P_U$ are affine. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], their fibre product is $\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_C A')$, which is $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ by step 7 (interchanging the tensor factors gives $b\otimes x\mapsto x\otimes b$). The agreement of the ring maps in step 7 shows that this is the restriction of $\theta$, not an unrelated isomorphism. Here restriction of a fibre product to an open of its base is the fibre product of the restricted schemes: a map to either object is exactly a compatible pair whose common composite factors through that open, by the defining universal property. The opens $R_U$ so obtained cover $R$, as the $P_U$ cover $P$. The inverse image $\theta^{-1}(R_U)$ is $V=a^{-1}U$, since $\theta$ is over $P$. Each local inverse is also over $P$, by composing its inverse equation with $R\to P$. Thus on $R_{U_1}\cap R_{U_2}$ both inverses land in $a^{-1}(U_1\cap U_2)$, where they invert the same restriction of $\theta$; uniqueness of inverses makes them equal. Scheme-morphism gluing gives a global inverse to $\theta$, with both inverse equations checked on these covers. Hence $T\cong S\times_P T'$. If $S$ is empty, the map $a$ forces $T$ empty and the homeomorphism $i$ forces $T'$ empty; the construction is the empty scheme and the same universal properties hold. All arguments also allow zero affine coordinate rings and thickenings whose ideal has no global nilpotence exponent.
